sourceEvidence.label: A90 WSTA ownership evidence, current contracts, H24 native source, and isolated-Debian design

assessment.summary: A clean Debian-supervised vendor WLAN capsule is a valid H0 research opportunity, but the reduced native-supervisor design remains the only live-supported baseline until the exact minimum service set, containment boundary, cold-relaunch behavior, recovery, and performance are proved.

nonNegotiables: H24 remains the exact installed healthy resident and its consumed D1 is never replayed.
Only boot may be a partition payload; UFS remains read-only and no direct filesystem-content mutation is authorized.
Exact rollback, physical recovery, durable no-replay, SD-free evidence, and final health remain mandatory.
Remote SSH and workload code never becomes the privileged WLAN platform owner.
A90 evidence, authority, profiles, and commands do not transfer to S22+ or S20+.
assumptions: The public WSTA reports accurately preserve their historical live results; private raw artifacts were not reread.
The current H24 service-object-visible branch is accumulated source behavior; H24 never reached it live, so it is neither live-qualified nor known-minimal.
No measured latency, memory, power, wakeup, or recovery comparison exists for the proposed alternatives.
Single owner means one steady-state lifecycle and policy authority, not one process or the absence of a vendor hardware backend.

opportunities.title: Make the persistent WLAN backend single-owner without losing WCNSS/WMI
opportunities.summary: Determine whether Debian PID 1 can cleanly supervise a minimal manifest-bound vendor compatibility capsule while rootless services remain unable to name its privileged capabilities.
opportunities.diagnosis: WSTA18 refutes only the disappearance of vendor userspace followed by passive wlan0 inheritance. Current H24 source shows a multi-service Android compatibility environment, while the selected design contains it behind a second native supervisor. The minimum vendor service set and its ability to relaunch under Debian are unproved.

evidence.claim: After full handoff, Debian retained wlan0, phy, and rfkill visibility while firmware, Root PD, and WMI stopped and the vendor service set was absent.
Native scan remained healthy while Debian Dropbear ran under the native-owned chroot model.

The H24-selected service-object-visible path constructs thirteen composite child entries representing eleven unique roles because servicemanager and hwservicemanager are each enqueued twice; it also maintains a property-service shim and subsystem-modem holder.
The H24 property snapshot source is compiled under /mnt/sdext and cannot be inherited by an SD-free successor.
Preserving privileged sidecars in a process view accessible to root-equivalent remote services would retain the old-root and FD capability class even if Debian becomes the supervisor.
A safe H24-equivalent reproduction needs distinct Android identities and IPC containment, but that negative design does not establish the minimum service set.

desiredInvariants: Exactly one steady-state lifecycle and policy authority exists: Debian PID 1.
The WLAN compatibility capsule has an exact finite dependency manifest and every member is justified by ablation or an explicit dependency proof.
Every capsule process clean-execs without a native old root, cwd, directory FD, file or device mapping, secret mapping, namespace handle, or unbounded environment.
Every capsule member has exact identities, capabilities, SELinux behavior, scheduler state, resources, FDs, devices, socket families, paths, and IPC endpoints.
Remote SSH and workload identities cannot name, signal, ptrace, duplicate, configure, or persist any capsule capability.
No SD, generic Android root bind, mutable vendor partition, native devtmpfs, userdata block, or unmanifested firmware and RFS input is reachable.
Station, association, DHCP, route, and resolver policy have one explicit owner and their evidence is not conflated with backend readiness.
Durable intent precedes every effect, uncertain accept is never replayed, and cleanup preserves original failure attribution.
Rollback, physical recovery, attended return, and final native health semantics remain exact.
Performance and resources are measured against an identical reduced-native baseline before selection.

options.title: Reduced native supervisor and isolated Debian
options.summary: Keep the selected ownership topology while reducing native production duties and the vendor service set to an exact manifest.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: The vendor backend remains alive instead of being removed at handoff.
It preserves the live-supported native-owned topology.
Nested PID and matching procfs isolation are still required before a successor can exist.
Ablation can reduce the service tree, but the architecture does not eliminate it.

tradeoffs.assessment: The selected namespace and veth boundary keeps remote Debian services away from vendor devices and IPC, while explicit native reduction narrows the TCB.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Complete the selected-design negative corpus and prove the native reachable closure contains only WLAN, supervision, evidence, cleanup, power, and recovery.

tradeoffs.assessment: The veth and filtering path adds hops and copies, but the cost has not been measured.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure p50 and p95 local throughput, latency, CPU time, and authenticated SSH readiness against a direct-network alternative.

tradeoffs.assessment: Two namespace roots, a native supervisor, and a Debian PID 1 remain resident; exact RSS and PSS are unknown.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Capture exact process counts and smaps_rollup RSS and PSS after five idle minutes over twenty clean boots.

tradeoffs.assessment: The ownership shape follows WSTA19 through WSTA43 and avoids an unproved cold backend restart.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prove the isolated successor's WLAN backend, Debian local service, cleanup, fallback, and attended return independently.

tradeoffs.assessment: Operators must correlate two health planes and a cross-boundary network policy.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Require one canonical timeline that distinguishes backend, Debian, ingress, cleanup, and final-health states.

tradeoffs.assessment: It is closest to the selected H0 design and preserves the proven WLAN ownership model.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Implement only after current independent H0 review, then qualify a fresh identity with no H24 state reuse.

residualRisks: The native service set may remain larger than production needs.
Two supervisors and veth policy remain permanent execution-critical machinery.
No isolated-Debian successor has yet been implemented or live-proven.

workPackages: Derive and reduce the reachable native production closure.
Implement and independently qualify a fresh successor only after H0 passes.
acceptanceCriteria: Every selected-design invariant passes static, unarmed, and separately authorized live validation.
No HUD, general shell, SD property input, or ownership diagnostic remains reachable.
migrationNotes: H24 remains the starting resident; no H24 approval, enable path, latch, or evidence is reusable.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Use only the exact reviewed boot-only rollback and prove final native RESIDENT_HEALTHY.

options.title: Clean prelaunch and Debian adoption
options.summary: Start the final clean compatibility capsule before handoff to preserve backend continuity, then transfer sole steady-state supervision to Debian PID 1.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: Prelaunch avoids an intentional backend gap, but transfer behavior is unproved.
A clean final root and isolated remote workload are mandatory; adoption alone does not close proc capabilities.
The exact minimum capsule and its transferable control handles are unknown.

tradeoffs.assessment: A clean prelaunch can eliminate old-root inheritance, but an imprecise adoption protocol can retain privileged handles or reopen the shared-proc hazard.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prove clean maps and FDs, pidfd-bound adoption, exact control-handle transfer, workload isolation, and zero old-root capability.

tradeoffs.assessment: The backend can initialize in parallel before Debian exec and avoids a cold-restart gap.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Compare boot-to-backend-ready and boot-to-authenticated-SSH p50 and p95 with Option 1 over twenty clean boots.

tradeoffs.assessment: The native bootstrap exits, but the compatibility capsule remains; net savings depend on the minimum service set.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure steady capsule plus Debian RSS and PSS against the reduced native baseline.

tradeoffs.assessment: Backend continuity is attractive, but process adoption, alternate reaping, and crash prefixes add new failure modes.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Exercise crashes before and after every launch, accept, exec, adoption, and journal publication boundary with no replay.

tradeoffs.assessment: After adoption, one Debian supervisor can own the steady-state timeline.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prove all capsule children, health, and cleanup are visible through one bounded platform API without exposing them to SSH users.

tradeoffs.assessment: It requires a new clean capsule, adoption protocol, and workload boundary while preserving boot-time continuity.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Complete host-only dependency and adoption design reviews before any resident implementation.

residualRisks: The capsule may retain hidden launch-time state despite a clean root.
A crash around adoption can leave supervisor ownership uncertain.
Debian PID 1 can legitimately see the capsule, so remote workload separation remains essential.

workPackages: Design a durable no-replay launch and adoption state machine.
Prove clean root, maps, FDs, and control-handle lifetime.
acceptanceCriteria: No vendor process retains native old-root or unbound state.
Exactly one accepted adoption occurs and Debian proves full lifecycle control.
migrationNotes: Use only if clean cold relaunch is refuted and continuity is necessary.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Close ingress, terminate the exact capsule once, and return through the boot-only native rollback without a second adoption attempt.

options.title: Clean Debian relaunch
options.summary: Exec Debian PID 1 first, then launch a manifest-pinned vendor compatibility capsule before any station policy or external service ingress.

evidenceCoverage.rationale: WSTA18 proves passive inheritance fails but does not establish whether a clean cold relaunch can recover Root PD and WMI.
Native sidecars disappear, but the capsule and remote workload still require an internal capability boundary.
The current service tree must be reduced, rebuilt from clean inputs, and independently validated.
A new trace-derived positive policy is required for both the capsule and Debian platform manager.

tradeoffs.assessment: One lifecycle authority and clean capsule launch can remove the native proc/old-root boundary, but only if remote services are separately contained and the capsule receives exact capabilities.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Prove the desired invariants with positive syscall policies, private IPC, exact device and path manifests, and hostile rootless-workload tests.

tradeoffs.assessment: Removing veth may reduce data-plane cost while cold service and firmware reconstruction may increase boot latency.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure the frozen boot, backend, scan, authenticated SSH, and local data-plane metrics against Option 1.

tradeoffs.assessment: One supervisor exits, but Android libraries, private IPC, and a workload sandbox remain; the net effect depends on ablation.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Measure exact process count, shared and private RSS, PSS, slab impact, and namespace objects after five idle minutes.

tradeoffs.assessment: One supervisor simplifies steady-state recovery, but Root PD cold restart after WSTA18-style shutdown is unproved.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Separate backend cold-relaunch, station policy, DHCP, SSH, and cleanup proofs; stop on the first unproved stage.

tradeoffs.assessment: One PID 1 and one durable journal make lifecycle ownership and incident attribution easier to explain.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Require a single canonical timeline with distinct backend, station, IP, SSH, workload, cleanup, and recovery states.

tradeoffs.assessment: This option requires the largest source, rootfs, service, policy, and qualification program.
tradeoffs.validationPlan: Finish all H0 work packages and a separate target-contract review before allocating an identity.

residualRisks: Root PD and WMI may not recover without reboot after a full userspace gap.
The minimum capsule may still require most of Android Binder, property, QRTR, RFS, and identity machinery.
A trusted Debian platform manager can become a larger compromise target if remote workload isolation is incomplete.
Debian station-policy ownership after backend readiness remains unproved.

workPackages: Build the exact service and dependency graph.
Create a deterministic SD-free read-only compatibility manifest.
Design clean launch, containment, logging, cleanup, and recovery.
Derive positive syscall and IPC policies.
Freeze performance budgets and complete independent review.
acceptanceCriteria: A clean cold relaunch proves backend readiness without association or external traffic.
Debian later proves station and IP policy without native autoconnect.
Remote workload cannot name or control any capsule capability.
Every failure returns through exact cleanup or reviewed recovery without replay.
migrationNotes: Promote only after an H0 decision supersedes the selected design through independent target-contract review.
implementationReadiness.rollback: Use a fresh boot-only candidate with the exact prior resident as rollback; never mutate UFS content or reuse H24 state paths.

opportunities.recommendation: Keep the reduced native-supervisor design as the current production baseline. Run clean Debian relaunch as a separate H0 feasibility program; prefer it only after its minimum service closure, clean containment, cold-relaunch behavior, recovery, and measured budgets pass.

openQuestions: Which of the eleven unique H24 service-object-visible roles are individually necessary for WCNSS, Root PD, WMI, and bounded scan readiness, and why are two service-manager roles duplicated into thirteen entries?
Can Root PD and WMI cold-recover after the final vendor backend exits without a reboot?
Can a private Binder context and boot-private property input replace H24's current global-device and SD property sources?
Can Debian own station, association, DHCP, route, and resolver policy once only the vendor backend is preserved?
What rootless workload boundary keeps remote code from naming the privileged capsule under a Debian-owned platform?
Do the alternatives satisfy accepted boot, memory, wakeup, throughput, and recovery budgets?
